newsitem.title: GREECE: Motor Oil refinery charged over Greek oil spill.
newsitem.headline: Motor Oil refinery charged over Greek oil spill.

text.p: Greek authorities have charged officials of the Motor Oil refinery with causing a major oil spill near the Corinth canal after environmentalists slammed the company as a prime polluter and blockaded its port facilities.
More than 300 tonnes of crude oil were spilled in August as a tanker owned by Motor Oil was unloading at the company's docking facilities during a thunderstorm in the middle of the night.

The refinery's director, the loading manager, the captain of the ship and the first mate will be tried on charges of causing serious marine oil pollution because of negligence, according to a decision of the Corinth judicial council's decision obtained by Reuters on Tuesday.
"(They) are charged to be tried as responsible for causing, through negligence, the criminal act of seriously polluting the sea," the Corinth judicial council said.
They face up to five years in jail if convicted.
Motor Oil, jointly owned by Saudi Aramco and the Greek Vardinoyannis family, has already been fined 150 million drachmas ($650,000) by the Merchant Marine Ministry for the accident.
The company has rejected accusations that its safety measures are lax, saying they were beyond those required by Greek law, and blamed the accident on the sudden storm.
Initial reports said a lightning bolt struck dead a worker and the ship was detached from its moorings, breaking its loading pipe.
But in justifying the charges, the council said the ship was not properly docked and its mooring ropes had not been tight.
It also said that lack of communication between crews delayed shutting off the loading valve and resulted in more oil being spilled.
Greenpeace activists blockaded the refinery's port for 24 hours in November to protest over the spill and demanded that Greece introduce stricter laws against oil pollution.
They were forcibly removed by coast guard commandos, who cut through chains pinning them to mooring buoys and loading cranes.
A public prosecutor charged 17 Greenpeace members, including many foreigners, with trespass and hindering a public service.
Their trial was postponed last week until April 10. They face up to five years in jail if convicted.

"We want an immediate trial," Greenpeace activist and one of the defendants, Nikos Charalambidis, told Reuters. "We will show that the essence of our action was correct and that those who pollute the environment are the ones that should be on trial."

Greenpeace wants a ban on loading at night or in bad weather, stricter laws against oil pollution and more prevention measures. It says oil dispersants used after oil spills in Greece are toxic and should be forbidden.
